The paper revisits the cloud-crushing problem with radiative cooling, where a dense cloud interacts with a diffuse hot wind.
The authors find that the efficient radiative cooling of the mixed gas in the turbulent boundary layer can lead to the continuous growth of the dense cloud.
The Gronke-Oh criterion states that cloud growth occurs when the cooling time of the mixed gas is shorter than the cloud-crushing time.
The Li criterion states that cloud growth occurs when the cooling time of the hot gas is shorter than the predicted cloud lifetime.
For typical parameters (T_cl = 10^4 K, M = 1.0, χ = 100, n_cl = 0.1 cm^-3), the Gronke-Oh and Li radii are approximately 1.1 pc and 26.5 pc, respectively.
The authors' simulations agree with the Gronke-Oh criterion, where cloud growth occurs for cloud sizes larger than the Gronke-Oh radius.
Clouds smaller than the Gronke-Oh radius are ultimately destroyed, consistent with the Li criterion.
The authors observe the formation of a turbulent wake with intermediate densities and temperatures, where the cooling of the mixed gas leads to the growth of the dense cloud mass at late times.
In the absence of cooling, the dense/cold cloud is mixed into the hot wind over a few cloud-crushing timescales.
With cooling, larger clouds (a few times the Gronke-Oh radius) show a late-time increase in dense mass as the mixed gas in the boundary layer cools and accretes onto the cloud.
The simulation domain should be large enough that the mixed gas in the turbulent boundary layer is not lost through the boundaries.
Higher resolution simulations (up to 64 cells per cloud radius) are able to resolve the small-scale features and fractal-like structure of the turbulent wake more clearly.
The paper's findings have important implications for understanding the multiphase structure and dynamics of the circumgalactic medium, galactic/AGN outflows, and other astrophysical systems.
Future work should consider the impact of magnetic fields, thermal conduction, and self-gravity on the cloud-crushing problem with radiative cooling.
The discrepancy between the Gronke-Oh and Li criteria highlights the need for careful modeling of the radiative cooling processes in these systems.
